name: String of Pearls
description: Native to the dry regions of southwest Africa, String of Pearls is an unusual succulent featuring long, trailing stems adorned with spherical, pea-sized leaves that look exactly like strings of green beads or pearls - one of nature's most whimsical designs. Each "pearl" has a translucent window stripe that allows light to penetrate for photosynthesis. The delicate stems can trail 2-3 feet long, creating stunning cascading displays in hanging baskets. When happy, it produces small white flowers with a cinnamon-like fragrance. However, String of Pearls has a reputation for being finicky - the pearls drop easily when touched, it's prone to rot, and it requires specific watering and light conditions. Success requires understanding its needs, but the enchanting appearance makes it worth the effort for patient growers.
toxicity: Toxic to cats and dogs. Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids; eating it can cause vomiting and diarrhea.
careInstructions: Water only when pearls show slight wrinkling - every 10-14 days typically
Water soil directly, never overhead - wet pearls rot easily
Provide bright, indirect light - direct sun can scorch the pearls
Use very well-draining succulent mix in shallow pot
Handle gently - pearls detach easily when touched
Propagate from stem cuttings laid on soil surface
Fertilize every 2-3 months during growing season with diluted fertilizer
Bottom watering method works well for this plant
commonProblems: Shriveling pearls: Needs water - water when slightly wrinkled
Mushy, translucent pearls: Overwatering causing rot - reduce watering
Pearl drop: Normal when touched, or from overwatering/underwatering
Stretching with spaces between pearls: Insufficient light
Bare stems near base: Natural growth pattern - trim and replant to fill in
Root rot: Most common cause of death - use well-draining soil

fertilizing.tip: Fertilize every 2-3 months during growing season with diluted fertilizer

repotting.tip: Repot each spring. After several years plants tend to die back — take cuttings and start fresh.
repotting.soil: Dry, sandy, cactus-type mix (or potting soil with sand or perlite)

whatsNormal: Plants tend to die back after several years; cuttings are the way to renew them.
Shriveled pearls mean the watering or light is off — too much or too little water, or not enough light.
Each pearl has a translucent stripe, a "window" that lets light inside.
The small white flowers smell like cinnamon.

propagation.tip: Lay 3-5 inch cuttings on the mix with a few nodes covered.

flags.note: Toxicity: not on the ASPCA lists. NC State describes it as toxic but doesn't rate cats, dogs and horses separately.
Winter watering interval (21 days) is our estimate — the sources only say to reduce watering from fall to late winter.
Cold threshold is frost (32°F) — both sources only say it is frost-intolerant.
Changed: temperature now shows the summer/winter ranges both sources give; light advice now warns direct sun scorches (NC State).
Watering — resolved by majority: MOBOT and Wisconsin say let it dry out completely between waterings; NC State says never let it dry out completely. Set to "fully dry".
Humidity — our catalog said it prefers dry air (30-50%); MOBOT says it is unaffected by high humidity. Now 30-60%, "average home humidity is fine".
